entry.title: Workshop Selection Using Dynamic Programming in Java

link.title: Workshop Selection Using Dynamic Programming in Java

entry.content:
Introduction

Every conference poses the same hidden optimization problem: the schedule is full of attractive workshops, several of them overlap, and you can only be in one room at a time. Each session has a different appeal — some are must-see, some are filler — so the goal is not to attend the most sessions, but to walk away with the most total value.

This post walks through a complete Java console application I built for my algorithms course that solves exactly this problem. It is the classic weighted interval scheduling problem, and the solution is a textbook application of dynamic programming: sort by finish time, compute predecessors, fill a DP table, and reconstruct the optimal schedule. Along the way we will see why the obvious greedy strategy fails, why the recurrence is correct, how the schedule is reconstructed from the DP table, and how the implementation was verified against brute force and benchmarked up to 5,000 workshops.

The Problem

The input is a CSV file of workshops. Each workshop has an id, a fixed start and finish time (stored as minutes after midnight, so 09:00 is 540), and a preference value:

id,start,finish,value
A,540,600,4
B,600,660,4
C,540,660,10

The task: select a subset of workshops such that no two selected workshops overlap and the sum of values is maximized. Two simplifying assumptions make the model clean: back-to-back sessions are allowed (a workshop ending at 10:00 and one starting at 10:00 do not conflict — zero travel time), and values are nonnegative and additive.

Why not just try every subset? Because there are 2^n of them. Twenty workshops already means a million combinations; a thousand workshops means a number with about 300 digits. We need something smarter.

Why Greedy Is Not Enough

The natural first instinct is a greedy rule: always take the workshop that finishes earliest. Intuitively it makes sense — finishing early keeps the rest of the day open. And in fact, if every workshop had the same value, this rule is provably optimal: it maximizes the count of sessions you can attend.

But our objective is total value, not count, and that changes everything. Look at the three workshops above:

Workshop Time Value
A 09:00–10:00 4
B 10:00–11:00 4
C 09:00–11:00 10

The greedy rule takes A first (it finishes earliest), then B (compatible with A), and skips C because it overlaps both. Total: 8. But the optimal answer is C alone: 10. The greedy choice of A — locally sensible, finishes first — irrevocably blocks the single most valuable workshop. No simple greedy rule can repair this, because a locally good choice can foreclose the global optimum. This is precisely the situation where dynamic programming earns its keep: instead of committing to one branch, it evaluates both options (take it or skip it) for every workshop, reusing subproblem solutions so the exploration never explodes.

The Algorithm

The algorithm has four steps. Everything below refers to workshops sorted by finish time, with 1-based indices.

Step 1 — Sort by finish time

Sort the workshops by finish time (breaking ties by id so results are reproducible). This ordering is the keystone: after sorting, all workshops compatible with workshop j — those that finish before j starts — form a contiguous prefix at the front of the list. That contiguity is what makes the recurrence possible.

Step 2 — The predecessor array p[j]

For each workshop j, define:

p[j] = the largest i < j such that finish[i] <= start[j] (or 0 if none)

In plain words: if I attend workshop j, what is the latest workshop I could have attended just before it? Because the list is sorted by finish time, scanning backwards from j−1 and stopping at the first compatible workshop automatically yields the largest such i.

The payoff of this definition is subtle and elegant: since compatible workshops form a prefix, “the best I can do with anything compatible with j” is exactly “the best I can do with the first p[j] workshops” — which is a subproblem the DP table already solves. p[j] is the bridge that connects the “include j” case to a solved subproblem.

Step 3 — The DP table

Let OPT[j] denote the maximum total value achievable using only the first j workshops. The base case is OPT[0] = 0 (the empty schedule). For j ≥ 1, every schedule for the first j workshops either contains workshop j or it does not:

OPT[j] = max( OPT[j-1],  v[j] + OPT[p[j]] )
  • Exclude j: the schedule lives entirely in the first j−1 workshops, worth at most OPT[j−1].
  • Include j: we gain v[j], and everything else must finish before j starts — so the rest is a schedule over the prefix ending at p[j], worth at most OPT[p[j]].

Why is taking the maximum of these two cases correct? By induction. When we compute OPT[j], both OPT[j−1] and OPT[p[j]] refer to smaller prefixes and are already optimal. Any optimal schedule falls into one of the two cases, so its value is bounded by the corresponding case — and both case values are achievable. Maximum of the two equals the optimum.

Step 4 — Reconstructing the schedule

OPT[n] gives the best value, but not which workshops achieve it. During the fill we record a boolean take[j] (true when including j strictly beat skipping it), then walk backwards from j = n:

  • if take[j]: workshop j belongs to the answer; jump to j = p[j] (everything between p[j] and j is incompatible with j anyway);
  • otherwise: workshop j is not used; step to j − 1.

The collected workshops are reversed at the end. One subtlety worth emphasizing: the answer is this single backtracking path, not “every j with take[j] = true”. The take[] array stores decisions from branches the final path never traverses, and blindly printing all of them produces a wrong schedule.

A Worked Example

Here is a four-workshop example, small enough to trace by hand but rich enough to exercise every branch of the algorithm:

ID Start Finish Value
A 09:00 10:00 6
B 10:00 11:00 2
C 10:00 12:00 8
D 11:30 12:30 5

Sorted by finish time the order is A, B, C, D. Computing predecessors:

  • p[1] = 0 — nothing exists before A.
  • p[2] = 1 — A finishes at 10:00 exactly when B starts: compatible (adjacency allowed).
  • p[3] = 1 — B finishes at 11:00, after C starts at 10:00; A is the latest compatible.
  • p[4] = 2 — C finishes at 12:00, after D starts at 11:30; B is the latest compatible.

Now the DP table:

j ID Select = v[j] + OPT[p[j]] Skip = OPT[j−1] take[j] OPT[j]
1 A 6 + OPT[0] = 6 0 true 6
2 B 2 + OPT[1] = 8 6 true 8
3 C 8 + OPT[1] = 14 8 true 14
4 D 5 + OPT[2] = 13 14 false 14

OPT = [0, 6, 8, 14, 14]. The best value is 14, and notice that at j = 4 skipping D wins — the algorithm compared both branches instead of committing to one, exactly what the greedy cannot do.

Reconstruction walks backwards: j = 4, take is false → skip D, go to j = 3. j = 3, take is true → C is selected, jump to p[3] = 1. j = 1, take is true → A is selected, jump to p[1] = 0. Done. The optimal schedule is A + C = 14.

And here is the subtlety from the previous section made concrete: take[2] is true (including B beat skipping it when only the first two workshops were considered), yet B is not in the final answer — the winning path went through C, which excludes B. Following the single backtracking path, with its jumps via p[j], is what keeps the reconstruction honest. On this same input the greedy takes A + B + D for a total of 13 — one point of value lost to a rule that cannot look ahead.

The Implementation

The project is deliberately split into seven small files, one responsibility each — which also makes each piece explainable in isolation:

File Responsibility
Workshop.java The data model: id, start, finish, value, and the overlap test
WorkshopCsv.java Read and validate the CSV; every bad row fails loudly with a line number
WeightedIntervalScheduler.java The algorithm: sort, predecessors, DP table, reconstruction, trace mode
GreedyBaseline.java The earliest-finish greedy, for comparison
ExhaustiveSearch.java Brute force over all 2^n subsets — the ground truth oracle (n ≤ 20)
ScheduleGenerator.java Seeded, reproducible synthetic schedules
Main.java The CLI: solve, verify, selftest, benchmark, generate

The core of the solver is short. The predecessor computation is a backward scan:

private static int[] computePredecessors(List<Workshop> sorted) {
    int n = sorted.size();
    int[] p = new int[n + 1];                 // p[0] = 0 sentinel

    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
        int startJ = sorted.get(j - 1).start;

        // Scan backwards from j-1 down to 1.
        for (int i = j - 1; i >= 1; i--) {
            if (sorted.get(i - 1).finish <= startJ) {
                p[j] = i;                     // largest compatible i
                break;                        // stop at the FIRST hit
            }
        }
    }
    return p;
}

And the DP fill is a direct translation of the recurrence:

for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
    Workshop w = sorted.get(j - 1);

    int include = w.value + opt[p[j]];   // case 2: attend workshop j
    int exclude = opt[j - 1];            // case 1: skip workshop j

    take[j] = include > exclude;         // strict '>' per the pseudocode
    opt[j] = Math.max(include, exclude);
}

A --trace flag prints the full DP table (j, p[j], skip, select, OPT[j]) so the walkthrough above can be reproduced live with:

java -cp out Main solve data/example_walkthrough.csv --trace

Verification: Trust, but Check

How do you know the DP is actually correct, and not just plausible? Three layers:

  1. Brute-force oracle. For small inputs (n ≤ 20) the program enumerates all 2^n subsets, keeps the conflict-free ones, and returns the true optimum. On every tested instance — the edge-case CSVs and five seeded random instances — the DP value equals the exhaustive value. This is the strongest check available: not “the answer looks right” but “the answer is provably the best of everything”.

  2. Structural checks. For every solution the tests also verify that the selected schedule is genuinely conflict-free (pairwise overlap test) and that the reported value equals the sum of the selected values — the reconstruction cannot invent value.

  3. Edge cases. Empty input, a single workshop, no overlaps at all, everything overlapping, ties in finish times, zero values, back-to-back sessions, and an invalid CSV row (start after finish) that must be rejected with a clear error. The selftest runs all of it in one command:

java -cp out Main selftest data
# SELFTEST RESULT: 14 passed, 0 failed

The synthetic generator deserves a mention here because of reproducibility: it uses an explicitly seeded java.util.Random, so the same parameters always regenerate the identical file. Every experiment below can be replayed by anyone, bit for bit.

Benchmark Results

The benchmark generates instances with a fixed overlap parameter of 0.6 (start times compressed into roughly the first three hours of the day, so conflicts are frequent but the problem is not trivial), for sizes 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 workshops, with three fixed seeds each. Runtime is the median of five runs after a warm-up, to shield the measurement from JIT compilation and garbage-collection noise:

n       seed   DP value   DP ms     Greedy ms  Greedy val  Gap
100     7      82         0.226     0.094      60          22
500     7      106        0.688     0.199      70          36
1000    7      113        0.668     0.228      57          56
5000    7      119        12.160    1.347      84          35

Two observations fall out of this table:

  • The value gap is real and systematic. The DP beats the greedy on every seed and every size, often by 30–50% of the greedy’s value. The “obvious” rule leaves a lot of preference points on the table.
  • The runtime grows quadratically, as the theory predicts. From n = 500 to n = 5,000 (ten times the workshops) the DP time grows roughly thirty-fold — the signature of the O(n²) predecessor scan, which at n = 5,000 performs about 12.5 million cheap comparisons, still finishing in ~12 ms.

Complexity

Operation Cost
Sort by finish time O(n log n)
Compute all predecessors (backward scan) O(n²)
Fill DP table + reconstruct schedule O(n)
Total time O(n²)
Memory O(n) (the p, OPT, and take arrays)

The dominant term is the predecessor scan. Because finish times are sorted, each p[j] query could instead be answered with a binary search over the finish array, bringing the total down to O(n log n). I kept the O(n²) scan deliberately: it matches the project proposal, it is trivially explainable line by line, and at these input sizes the difference is milliseconds. The comparison worth remembering is not O(n²) versus O(n log n) — it is O(n²) versus the O(2^n) of brute force, which is the difference between 12 milliseconds and a number of centuries no one should ever compute.

Conclusion

Weighted interval scheduling is one of those problems where the journey is the lesson. The greedy rule fails for a reason that generalizes far beyond scheduling: local optimality is not global optimality when choices constrain the future. The fix — dynamic programming — works because sorting by finish time turns “everything compatible with j” into a contiguous prefix, p[j] turns that prefix into an address, and the recurrence OPT[j] = max(skip, take) reduces an exponential search to n comparisons of two already-solved subproblems.

The full source (seven Java files, ten sample CSVs, and a README with a class-demo script) is compact enough to read in one sitting — and if you want to watch the DP think, run the solver with --trace and follow the table row by row. It is a rare pleasure in algorithms: an optimal answer you can watch being built, one decision at a time.

entry.title: Solving Exercism’s Secret Handshake in Java

link.title: Solving Exercism’s Secret Handshake in Java

entry.content:
The Problem

Exercism’ Secret Handshake exercise looks mysterious at first: you receive an integer, and you must return a list of handshake actions. The trick is that the answer is hidden in the binary representation of the number, not in the number itself. Here is my code.

The five least-significant bits each have a meaning:

Bit Value Action
0 1 wink
1 2 double blink
2 4 close your eyes
3 8 jump
4 16 reverse the list

The first four bits add their action to the list, in that fixed order. The fifth bit does not add anything: if it is set, the final list gets reversed.

A few examples to make it concrete:

  • 1 → 00001 → bit 0 set → [wink]
  • 3 → 00011 → bits 0 and 1 → [wink, double blink]
  • 19 → 10011 → bits 0, 1, 4 → [double blink, wink] (reversed)
  • 26 → 11010 → bits 1, 3, 4 → [jump, double blink] (reversed)

My Approach

The key insight is recognizing what kind of problem this is. Each bit is simply a yes/no flag: “is this action in the list or not?” There is no arithmetic, no recursion, no parsing. Once you see the input as five independent flags, the solution almost writes itself.

The approach is three steps:

  1. Mask the input to keep only the five bits we care about. Anything above bit 4 is irrelevant, so I clear it away immediately with number & 0b1_1111 (that is 31, i.e. 2⁵ − 1). This also guarantees the value is between 0 and 31 no matter what integer the caller passes.
  2. Test each bit with the bitwise AND. The expression (code & 0b00010) != 0 asks a single, precise question: “is bit 1 set?” If yes, add the matching action to the list.
  3. Reverse if bit 4 is set, using the standard library’s Collections.reverse().

Why (code & mask) != 0 works: AND compares two numbers bit by bit and keeps a 1 only where both have one. So AND-ing with a mask that has a single 1 isolates exactly that bit — the result is non-zero only if the bit is set:

  26 = 11010
&  2 = 00010   ← mask for "double blink"
──────────────
       00010   ← non-zero: bit 1 IS set

  26 = 11010
&  1 = 00001   ← mask for "wink"
──────────────
       00000   ← zero: bit 0 is NOT set

The Solution

The exercise expects a HandshakeCalculator class and a Signal enum. I like keeping the actions in an enum rather than raw strings — the compiler then guarantees there are no typos and no invalid values:

enum Signal {
    WINK, DOUBLE_BLINK, CLOSE_YOUR_EYES, JUMP
}

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

class HandshakeCalculator {

    List<Signal> calculateHandshake(int number) {
        List<Signal> signals = new ArrayList<>();
        int code = number & 0b1_1111;

        if ((code & 0b00001) != 0) {
            signals.add(Signal.WINK);
        }
        if ((code & 0b00010) != 0) {
            signals.add(Signal.DOUBLE_BLINK);
        }
        if ((code & 0b00100) != 0) {
            signals.add(Signal.CLOSE_YOUR_EYES);
        }
        if ((code & 0b01000) != 0) {
            signals.add(Signal.JUMP);
        }
        if ((code & 0b10000) != 0) {
            Collections.reverse(signals);
        }

        return signals;
    }
}

Tracing 26 through it: 26 & 31 is still 26 (11010). Bit 0 → off, skip. Bit 1 → set, add DOUBLE_BLINK. Bit 2 → off, skip. Bit 3 → set, add JUMP. Bit 4 → set, so reverse: [JUMP, DOUBLE_BLINK]. Done.

Complexity

Time: O(1). The method does one masking AND, four fixed bit checks, at most four list additions, and possibly one reversal of at most four elements. That is the same amount of work whether the input is 1 or 2,147,483,647. There are no loops over the input and nothing that grows with its value.

Space: O(1). The result list holds at most four elements regardless of the input, so the extra memory is bounded by a constant.

Constant time and space is possible here because the problem has a fixed, bounded universe: exactly five relevant bits and four possible actions. There is nothing to scale. A tempting alternative — converting the number to a binary string and reading characters — would also pass the tests, but it hides the intent behind string allocations and character parsing, while each bitwise check here maps to a single CPU instruction.

Takeaways

  • The right representation makes code trivial: 26 looks arbitrary, 11010 tells the whole story.
  • (value & (1 << i)) != 0 is the idiomatic bit test in Java — worth knowing by heart.
  • Collections.reverse() reverses in place, in O(n), and the standard library is the right place to look before writing your own.
  • When a problem has a fixed number of flags, expect O(1): recognizing why is more valuable than the solution itself.
entry.summary: A compact walkthrough of the Secret Handshake exercise: how to read bits, build the answer, and why the whole thing runs in constant time.

entry.title: Software Testing in Java: A Practical Guide to JUnit 5

link.title: Software Testing in Java: A Practical Guide to JUnit 5

entry.content:
I will be honest with you: for a long time I treated tests as something you write after the code is done — a boring step you rush through before pushing to the repo. If you ever thought the same, this post is for you.

At some point it clicked for me: testing is not a chore you do after coding. It is part of coding itself. This post is the guide I wish I had read back then — short on theory, long on examples.

Why Bother Writing Tests?

Picture the typical “no tests” workflow: you change a method, run the app, click through a few screens, and convince yourself everything works. It feels fast. The problem is that it does not scale:

  • Manual checking gets slower over time. Every new feature adds more things you should re-check by hand.
  • A well-written test catches a bug in milliseconds. A missing test lets that bug reach production and your users.
  • Tests give you confidence. When the suite is green, you can refactor and add features without the fear of silently breaking something.

The habit feels slower at first, then quietly makes everything faster.

The Map: Four Levels of Testing

Testing happens at different levels. Knowing the map keeps you oriented:

Level What It Tests Example Who Runs It
Unit One method or class, in isolation “does add(2, 3) return 5?” Developers
Integration Components working together “does UserService save via the repository correctly?” Developers
System The whole application against requirements “can a user complete checkout end to end?” QA team
Acceptance Real user/business needs “does this actually solve the user’s problem?” Stakeholders

As a developer, you own the first two levels. That is where this post — and JUnit — live.

A few extra terms you will hear: regression testing (re-running the suite to catch anything broken by new changes), smoke testing (a quick sanity check on critical paths after a build), performance testing (behavior under load), and exploratory testing (unscripted, curiosity-driven probing). You do not need them daily, but recognizing the words helps.

Setting Up JUnit 5

JUnit 5 is the standard testing framework for Java. One dependency and you are ready.

Maven (pom.xml):

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>5.10.2</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Gradle (build.gradle):

testImplementation 'org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.10.2'

Your First Test

Here is the class we want to test:

public class Calculator {
    public int add(int a, int b)      { return a + b; }
    public int divide(int a, int b)   { return a / b; }
}

And here is its test class:

import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class CalculatorTest {

    private Calculator calculator;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        calculator = new Calculator();   // fresh object for every test
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("4 + 6 should equal 10")
    void testAdd() {
        assertEquals(10, calculator.add(4, 6));
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Dividing by zero should throw ArithmeticException")
    void testDivideByZero() {
        assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> calculator.divide(10, 0));
    }
}

Reading it line by line:

  • @Test marks a method as a test — you can have as many as you want.
  • @DisplayName gives the test a human-readable name in the report.
  • assertEquals(expected, actual) compares two values.
  • assertThrows(Exception.class, () -> ...) checks that running that code throws the given exception.
  • @BeforeEach runs before every single test, giving each one a fresh Calculator.

The golden rule behind @BeforeEach: never share mutable state between tests. Each test should start from a clean slate, so a failure always points at one specific problem.

The Full Lifecycle

JUnit models the life of a test explicitly. The five annotations, in order:

Annotation When It Runs Typical Use
@BeforeAll Once, before all tests in the class Expensive setup (start a server)
@BeforeEach Before every test method Fresh objects and state
@Test The test itself Your assertions
@AfterEach After every test method Cleanup
@AfterAll Once, after all tests Expensive teardown

The Assertions You Actually Need

Assertions are the vocabulary of tests. These six cover almost everything:

Assertion Question It Answers Example
assertEquals(x, y) Are these equal? assertEquals(10, calc.add(4, 6));
assertTrue(cond) Is this true? assertTrue(result > 0);
assertFalse(cond) Is this false? assertFalse(list.isEmpty());
assertNull(x) / assertNotNull(x) Is this null / not null? assertNotNull(user);
assertThrows(Ex.class, () -> ...) Does this throw? assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> calc.divide(1, 0));
assertAll(...) Do all of these checks hold? see below

One nuance worth knowing — plain assertEquals calls stop at the first failure, so you fix one thing at a time. assertAll() runs every assertion inside it and reports all failures at once:

@Test
void testMultiply() {
    int result = calculator.multiply(3, 4);
    assertAll("multiply checks",
        () -> assertNotNull(result),
        () -> assertTrue(result > 0),
        () -> assertEquals(12, result)
    );
}

When a test fails, seeing all three broken expectations at once saves you two extra run-fix cycles.

Parameterized Tests: One Test, Many Inputs

Copying and pasting a test method for every input combination gets old fast. @ParameterizedTest writes the logic once and feeds it data:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} + {1} = {2}")
@CsvSource({
    "1,  2,  3",
    "5,  5, 10",
    "-3, 3,  0",
    "0,  0,  0"
})
void testAdd(int a, int b, int expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, calculator.add(a, b));
}

The @CsvSource table maps each row to the method parameters: the first row runs testAdd(1, 2, 3), the second testAdd(5, 5, 10), and so on. Four test runs, one method.

For single-argument tests, @ValueSource is even simpler:

@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(ints = {1, 2, 3, 100, -5})
void testAddZero(int number) {
    assertEquals(number, calculator.add(number, 0));
}

Rule of thumb: the same logic with different data → parameterized test. Different logic → different test method.

Grouping with @Nested

When a test class grows, @Nested classes group related tests into a readable hierarchy:

@DisplayName("Calculator")
class CalculatorNestedTest {

    private final Calculator calculator = new Calculator();

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("addition")
    class AdditionTests {
        @Test void positiveNumbers() { assertEquals(5, calculator.add(2, 3));  }
        @Test void negativeNumbers() { assertEquals(-5, calculator.add(-2, -3)); }
    }

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("division")
    class DivisionTests {
        @Test void dividesNumbers() { assertEquals(2, calculator.divide(10, 5)); }
        @Test void divideByZero()   { assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class,
                                                  () -> calculator.divide(5, 0)); }
    }
}

In the IDE’s test tree this renders as Calculator → addition → positiveNumbers — it reads like a specification.

Mocking with Mockito

Real classes have dependencies: a UserService needs a UserRepository. In a unit test you do not want a real database — so you replace the dependency with a mock: a fake object you fully control.

Mockito is the standard library for this:

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class UserServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private UserRepository userRepository;  // fake repository

    @InjectMocks
    private UserService userService;        // real service, with the fake injected

    @Test
    void getUserById_returnsUser() {
        User user = new User(1, "Mario");

        // given: the mock returns Mario when asked for id 1
        when(userRepository.findById(1)).thenReturn(Optional.of(user));

        // when + then
        User result = userService.getUserById(1);

        assertEquals("Mario", result.getName());
        verify(userRepository, times(1)).findById(1);  // interaction was really used
    }
}

Four pieces to remember:

  • @Mock creates the fake.
  • @InjectMocks puts the fake into the real class under test.
  • when(...).thenReturn(...) scripts the fake’s behavior.
  • verify(...) checks the fake was actually called — testing the interaction, not just the result.

The TDD Loop

Everything above becomes even more powerful when you flip the order: write the test before the code. That is Test-Driven Development, and the loop is just three steps:

  1. Red — write a test for behavior that does not exist yet; watch it fail.
  2. Green — write the minimum code needed to make it pass.
  3. Refactor — clean up freely, knowing the test protects you.

Writing the test first forces you to think about what the code should do before thinking how. You end up with smaller methods, clearer responsibilities, and a suite that grows with the code instead of being retrofitted later.

Running Your Tests

  • IntelliJ / Eclipse: right-click the test class (or single method) → Run.
  • Maven: mvn test — report in target/surefire-reports.
  • Gradle: gradle test — report in build/reports/tests.

Cheat Sheet

I want to… Use
Check a value assertEquals(expected, actual)
Check an exception assertThrows(Ex.class, () -> ...)
Run many input combinations @ParameterizedTest + @CsvSource / @ValueSource
Reset state before each test @BeforeEach
See all failures at once assertAll(...)
Group related tests @Nested
Replace a dependency with a fake @Mock + @InjectMocks + when(...)
Check a dependency was called verify(mock)
Structure development Red → Green → Refactor

Writing tests is one of those habits that feels slower at first and then quietly makes everything faster. The codebase stays cleaner, refactoring stops being scary, and bugs get caught before anyone else sees them. Your future self — staring at a green pipeline at 11pm before a release — will be grateful.
entry.summary: A practical, example-driven guide to testing in Java — the testing landscape, JUnit 5 basics, assertions, parameterized tests, Mockito, and the TDD loop.

entry.title: My Coding Best Practices
entry.content:
Every developer, at some point, opens a file they wrote six months ago and wonders what they were thinking. The code works — technically — but it’s hard to read, harder to change, and terrifying to touch. I’ve been there too.

Over time, I built a set of practices that I apply every time I sit down to write code. They’re not rules I follow blindly — they’re habits I developed by making mistakes, reading other people’s code, and slowly learning what makes a codebase a pleasure to work in rather than a burden. This post is my attempt to write them all down in one place.

None of these are language-specific. Whether you write Java, Python, or JavaScript, the underlying principles are the same.

1. Use a Proper IDE

Before writing a single line of code, set yourself up with the right environment. An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is not just a text editor — it’s a tool that understands your code. It autocompletes method names and imports as you type, highlights errors before you even run the program, lets you rename a variable across the entire codebase in one operation, and integrates with Git so you never have to leave the editor to commit or review changes.

That removed friction adds up. The less time you spend fighting your tools, the more mental space you have for logic and design — which is where the real work happens.

Here are the tools worth knowing:

Language IDE Notes
Any VS Code Free, open source, highly extensible via plugins
Java IntelliJ IDEA Community Free, best-in-class Java support
Python PyCharm Community Free, excellent Python tooling
Any Eclipse Free, open source, mature ecosystem
Any Neovim Free, keyboard-driven, highly configurable

If you use VS Code, three extensions are worth installing from day one:

  • GitLens — rich Git history and inline blame annotations
  • SonarLint — real-time code quality and security analysis
  • Error Lens — displays errors and warnings inline, right next to the code

2. Write Code for Humans First

The machine doesn’t care what you name your variables. Your colleagues — and your future self — very much do. Code is read far more often than it is written, so always optimize for the reader.

// Hard to read — what does this do?
public double calc(double a, int b, double c) {
    return a * b * (1 - c);
}

// Clear — reads almost like a sentence
public double calculateFinalPrice(double unitPrice, int quantity, double discountRate) {
    return unitPrice * quantity * (1 - discountRate);
}

The second version needs no comment to be understood. That clarity is a choice, and it’s one worth making every time.

A few rules of thumb to keep in mind:

  • Variable names should explain what they store, not how (userList, not data)
  • Method names should describe what they do (sendWelcomeEmail(), not process())
  • Keep methods short — if a method doesn’t fit on one screen, it probably does too much

Tools like SonarQube Community Edition, PMD, and Checkstyle can help enforce these standards automatically across a Java project.

3. The SOLID Principles

As a codebase grows, it tends to rot in predictable ways: classes that accumulate responsibilities over time, code that breaks when you try to extend it, dependencies that are impossible to swap out for testing. SOLID is a set of five design principles that address exactly these failure modes.

Principle What It Means Practical Example
Single Responsibility A class should do one thing only UserValidator validates; it does not save to the database
Open/Closed Open for extension, closed for modification Add new behaviour via new classes, not by editing existing ones
Liskov Substitution Subclasses must be usable wherever their parent is used A Square subclass should not break code written for a Rectangle
Interface Segregation Prefer many small, focused interfaces over one large one Printable and Serializable as separate interfaces, not one Utility
Dependency Inversion Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations Inject a DatabaseInterface, not a specific MySQLDatabase

Each of these principles deserves more space than a table can give them. I’ll go deeper into each one with practical Java examples in a dedicated follow-up post.

4. Don’t Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears in two places, it will eventually be updated in one and forgotten in the other. This is one of the most common sources of subtle, hard-to-trace bugs.

// Bad — the same logic duplicated in two different places
String email = input.trim().toLowerCase(); // in the registration flow
String email = input.trim().toLowerCase(); // in the password reset flow

// Good — extracted once, reused everywhere
private String normalizeEmail(String input) {
    return input.trim().toLowerCase();
}

Every piece of logic should have a single, authoritative home in the codebase. When it needs to change — and it will — you change it in exactly one place and can be confident the fix propagates everywhere it needs to.

5. Comment Why, Not What

The code already shows what it does. A good comment explains why a non-obvious decision was made. Commenting obvious things creates noise that drowns out the comments that actually matter.

// Bad — the code already says this
i = i + 1; // increment i

// Good — explains a non-obvious constraint
i += 1; // offset by 1 because the external API uses 1-based indexing

Three rules to follow:

  • Comment on business rules, edge cases, and non-obvious algorithmic choices
  • Never comment out dead code — delete it. Git keeps the history
  • Always update a comment when you update the code it describes. A wrong comment is worse than no comment

6. Handle Errors Explicitly

Silent failures are a debugging nightmare. When something goes wrong and nothing is logged, you have no idea where to start looking.

// Bad — the error is swallowed silently
try {
    result = fetchUserData(userId);
} catch (Exception e) {
    // nothing
}

// Good — caught specifically, logged with context, re-thrown meaningfully
try {
    result = fetchUserData(userId);
} catch (NetworkException e) {
    logger.error("Failed to fetch user {}: {}", userId, e.getMessage(), e);
    throw new ServiceUnavailableException("User data temporarily unavailable", e);
}

Key habits:

  • Always catch the most specific exception type you can — a bare catch (Exception e) hides bugs
  • Log errors with enough context to reconstruct what happened: include IDs, inputs, and the original exception
  • Never expose raw stack traces to end users
  • Define custom exception classes to distinguish different failure modes from each other

7. Use Git — and Use It Well

Git is not just a backup tool. It is a communication tool. Your commit history tells the story of your project and lets anyone — including future you — understand why a decision was made months after the fact.

# Bad — tells you nothing
git commit -m "fix stuff"

# Good — tells you exactly what changed and why
git commit -m "fix: handle null user in authentication flow"

Conventional Commits is a lightweight standard worth adopting. The prefixes you’ll use most often are feat: for new features, fix: for bug fixes, refactor: for code restructuring without behaviour change, docs: for documentation updates, and test: for anything test-related.

Pull Requests

A Pull Request (PR) is a formal proposal to merge a branch of code into another — usually main. When you open one, you give teammates the chance to review your changes line by line, ask questions, and run automated checks via CI/CD before anything reaches the main branch. Even on solo projects, opening a PR and reviewing your own diff before merging catches a surprising number of obvious mistakes.

Keep PRs small and focused — 200 to 400 lines is a good target. Large PRs don’t get reviewed carefully; they get rubber-stamped. And three non-negotiable rules: never commit directly to main, never commit secrets or passwords, and always add sensitive files to .gitignore.

Two tools worth adding to your workflow:

  • pre-commit — run linting, formatting, and secret scanning automatically before every commit
  • act — run your GitHub Actions pipeline locally before pushing

8. Test Your Code

Untested code is code you cannot safely change. Tests are what give you the confidence to refactor, upgrade dependencies, and ship features without fear.

There are three levels of testing:

  • Unit tests — test individual methods in isolation. Fast and precise. This is a developer’s primary responsibility
  • Integration tests — verify that separate components work correctly together (a service correctly calling a repository, for example)
  • End-to-end tests — validate the full user flow from input to output

A quick example in Java with JUnit:

@Test
public void testCalculateFinalPrice_basicCase() {
    // $10 item, 3 units, 10% discount → $27.00
    assertEquals(27.00, calculator.calculateFinalPrice(10.0, 3, 0.10), 0.001);
}

@Test
public void testCalculateFinalPrice_noDiscount() {
    assertEquals(30.00, calculator.calculateFinalPrice(10.0, 3, 0.0), 0.001);
}

@Test
public void testCalculateFinalPrice_fullDiscount() {
    assertEquals(0.0, calculator.calculateFinalPrice(10.0, 3, 1.0), 0.001);
}

If you’re afraid to refactor something, that’s a signal you need more tests. Tests should be fast, isolated, and deterministic — no random data, no network calls, no shared state between test cases.

Language Testing Framework Mocking Library
Java JUnit 5 Mockito
JavaScript Jest Built-in
Python pytest unittest.mock

9. Automate Formatting and Linting

Inconsistent formatting is cognitive noise. When a codebase mixes tabs and spaces, or uses different brace styles across different files, every code review becomes a style debate instead of a logic discussion. The solution: automate it and never discuss it again.

The two tools you need are a formatter and a linter, and they do different things.

A formatter is purely cosmetic. It rewrites your code to conform to a consistent visual style — indentation, spacing, line breaks, brace placement. It doesn’t care about what your code does, only how it looks. You run it, and the file comes out formatted the same way every time, regardless of who wrote it.

A linter goes deeper. It analyzes your source code without executing it, looking for things that are technically valid but likely wrong: an unused variable, a function that’s grown too complex, a pattern known to cause bugs, a potential null pointer, a security vulnerability. It works by parsing your code into a structured representation and checking it against a set of rules — then reporting exactly which line violates which rule and why. Think of it as a second pair of eyes that never gets tired and never misses the same mistake twice.

Together, a formatter handles style and a linter handles quality. Both run automatically, no human judgement required.

Language Formatter Linter
Java google-java-format Checkstyle
JavaScript Prettier ESLint
Python Black Ruff

Add both to your CI/CD pipeline so they run automatically on every PR. If they’re not automated, they won’t be consistent.

10. Refactor Continuously

“Always leave the code cleaner than you found it.”

Good code is not written once and left alone — it is refined over time. Small, continuous refactors prevent technical debt from accumulating into an unmaintainable mess.

The signals are usually obvious: a method with more than three or four parameters, the same logic in multiple places, a class that has grown past two or three hundred lines, or that vague anxiety you feel before touching a particular file. When you notice any of these, take a few minutes to clean it up before moving on.

You don’t need a dedicated refactoring sprint. A few minutes of cleanup every time you touch a file is enough to keep a codebase healthy over the long term.

11. Don’t Optimize Prematurely

“Premature optimization is the root of all evil.” — Donald Knuth

The correct priority order is always: make it work → make it clear → make it fast. Optimizing before you have a measured performance problem leads to complex, hard-to-read code that solves a problem you don’t actually have.

Write the clearest solution first. Then, if performance becomes an issue, use a profiler to find where the real bottleneck is, and optimize only that specific part.

Don't guess. Measure.

Profiling tools worth knowing: VisualVM and async-profiler for Java, Chrome DevTools Performance panel for JavaScript, and py-spy for Python.

12. Separate Your Concerns

Keep different responsibilities in different parts of your code. The classic pattern is a three-layer architecture:

Presentation layer   →  handles input and output (UI, API endpoints)
Business logic layer →  contains the rules of your application
Data layer           →  handles storage and retrieval

When these layers bleed into each other — database queries inside UI components, business rules scattered across API handlers — you end up with classes that are impossible to test, reuse, or safely change. The boundary between layers doesn’t need to be rigid, but it does need to exist and be respected.

13. Never Hardcode Configuration

Hardcoding URLs, credentials, feature flags, or environment-specific values in source code is both a security risk and a maintenance problem.

// Bad — credentials in source code
Connection db = DriverManager.getConnection(
    "jdbc:postgresql://prod-server/mydb", "admin", "secret123"
);

// Good — read from the environment at runtime
String dbUrl = System.getenv("DATABASE_URL");
Connection db = DriverManager.getConnection(dbUrl);

Store secrets in .env files locally — always listed in .gitignore. In production, use environment variables or a dedicated secret manager. Useful libraries for loading .env files: dotenv-java for Java, dotenv for JavaScript, and python-dotenv for Python. For production secrets at scale, HashiCorp Vault is the open source standard.

14. Take Code Review Seriously

Code reviews exist not just to catch bugs, but to share knowledge and raise the quality standard of the whole team. How you participate on both sides matters.

As an author: keep PRs small and focused, explain non-obvious choices in the PR description, and review your own diff before requesting a review — you’ll catch most obvious mistakes yourself.

As a reviewer: ask questions instead of issuing directives. “Could this be null here?” lands better than “This will crash.” Approve good-enough code — perfect is the enemy of shipped — and make a point of noting good patterns, not only criticising bad ones.

15. How to Approach a Problem Before Writing Code

One of the most common mistakes developers make — especially early on — is opening the editor before they fully understand the problem. The result is code that solves the wrong thing, or solves the right thing in the wrong way, and has to be thrown away.

Here is the process I follow every time I need to solve something and translate it into code:

  1. Understand the problem fully before touching the keyboard. Read the requirements carefully. What is the input? What is the expected output? What are the edge cases — empty input, null values, very large data, invalid formats? Write these down. You cannot write a correct solution to a problem you haven’t fully understood.

  2. Break it down into smaller sub-problems. Almost every problem is a composition of simpler ones. Decompose it until each piece is small enough that you can describe it in one sentence. A function that does one clear, describable thing is a function you can write, test, and reason about.

  3. Think about the solution in plain language first. Before writing a single line of code, describe your approach in plain English — or pseudocode if you prefer. What data structures will you use? What is the order of operations? Where could things go wrong? If you can’t explain it clearly in words, you don’t understand it well enough to code it yet.

  4. Write the test before the implementation. Define what “correct” looks like before you try to be correct. Writing the test first forces you to think about the interface and behaviour of your code from the outside — which is exactly how users and other parts of the system will interact with it.

  5. Write the simplest solution that works. Resist the urge to be clever. The goal of the first version is correctness, not elegance. Get it working, verify it against your tests and edge cases, then look at whether it needs to be made clearer or faster.

  6. Refactor once it’s working. With a passing test suite as your safety net, you can now clean up freely. Extract repeated logic, rename things for clarity, simplify control flow. This is the step where good code is actually made.

The discipline here is resisting the pull to jump straight to step five. Spending five minutes thinking clearly at the start saves hours of confused debugging later.

Concepts Worth Understanding Deeply

Beyond day-to-day practices, these are the foundational ideas that will genuinely level up how you think about software. You don’t need to master all of them at once, but each one is worth spending time with:

  • Big O notation — reason about algorithm performance before profiling
  • Design patterns — Factory, Singleton, Observer, Strategy, Decorator. Shared vocabulary for common solutions
  • CAP theorem — fundamental trade-offs in distributed systems
  • ACID vs BASE — the two competing models for database transaction reliability
  • REST vs GraphQL — trade-offs between the two dominant API design philosophies
  • Immutability and pure functions — the foundation of functional programming and a powerful tool for eliminating side-effect bugs
  • Concurrency and race conditions — essential for writing correct multi-threaded or async code
  • The Twelve-Factor App — a methodology for building scalable, portable software (12factor.net)

These are not rules to follow blindly. They are principles developed by generations of developers through experience — and, more importantly, through mistakes. Start with the ones most relevant to your current project, apply them consistently, and build the habit from there.

The goal is not a perfect codebase. It’s a codebase that you and your team can read, understand, and confidently change six months from now. That’s the whole game.
